title: The Effect of Copper-Free, Low-Metal Molybdenum Disulfide Friction Pads on Carbon–Ceramic Friction Pads
abstract: This study systematically investigated three types of low-metal friction pads with different molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) contents and analyzed their physicochemical properties and friction and wear performance. Test results show that the A2 specimen, containing 8% MoS2, exhibited the best overall physicochemical properties, with shear strength and compressive strength reaching 6.69 ± 0.52 MPa and 61.77 ± 1.56 MPa, respectively, while also demonstrating the best hydrophobicity. Under braking conditions, the A2 specimen exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction (0.41) and a significantly reduced wear rate; compared to the A0 specimen without MoS2 addition, wear was reduced by 50%. In summary, MoS2 shows great application potential and is expected to become one of the core solid lubricants for automotive brake pads.

title: Gaseous Brake Wear Emissions from Heavy-Duty and Light-Duty Vehicles
abstract: Abstract A few studies have identified gaseous emissions from brake wear, yet their quantification so far remains limited. With the goal to quantify gases emitted from brake wear, this study utilizes a high-resolution proton transfer reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometer (PTR-TOF-MS) for measurements. Four commercially available brake pad materials were tested on a pin-on-disc tribometer against gray cast iron. The results reveal that emissions of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) strongly depend on braking intensity and the material composition of the brake pads, with light-duty brake pads emitting more gases compared to heavy-duty formulations under comparable braking conditions. Laboratory emission factors for total VOCs were estimated at around 2.20 to 19.20 mg km–1 vehicle–1 by upscaling pin-on-disc emissions to vehicle scale emissions, while more environmentally relevant emission factors were estimated at around 1.58 to 15.26 mg VOC km–1 vehicle–1 using measured VOC/PM10 ratios and published emission factors for primary particles. The chemical composition is dominated by oxidized VOCs and nitrogen-containing organics. Because urban areas can experience elevated brake wear emissions due to high traffic density, these findings highlight the need for further study to determine realistic emission factors and assess the contribution of brake wear gases to air pollution and human health.

abstract: The use of asbestos as the main material in brake pad manufacturing has been discontinued due to its toxic nature and serious health risks, including asbestosis, mesothelioma, and lung cancer, thereby encouraging the development of safer and more environmentally friendly alternative materials. This study developed bio-composite brake pads based on mahogany wood powder as a natural fiber combined with brass powder, using polyester resin as the matrix binder and magnesium oxide as a reinforcing agent to enhance mechanical integrity. The fabrication process was carried out using a compaction method followed by sintering to achieve optimal bonding and densification. This research aimed to evaluate the effects of compaction pressure and variations in constituent composition on the wear resistance of the brake pads. Compaction pressures of 3000, 3200, and 3400 psi were applied with mahogany powder to brass powder ratios of 1:4 and 4:4. Wear tests were conducted on all fabricated specimens. The results showed that the highest specific wear value of 9.2 × 10⁻⁴ mm³/kg.m occurred in the 1:4 composition at a compaction pressure of 3000 psi, while the lowest value of 5.5 × 10⁻⁴ mm³/kg.m was obtained in the 4:4 composition at a compaction pressure of 3400 psi. These findings indicate that both compaction pressure and constituent composition significantly affect the wear resistance of brake pads.

title: Supplementary material from "Intensity perception of time-compensated frictional changes"
abstract: Frictional cues are essential to dexterous manipulation and surface exploration. This study explores how humans rate the intensity of brief reductions in friction induced by ultrasonic lubrication; the tested pulses are time-compensated in that the integral of the displacement amplitude that stimulates the finger is constant, but with varying maximum amplitude and starting/ending transition duration. The results show that both amplitude and transition time significantly influence how intense a frictional change feels, and that a very sharp ultrasonic stimulation with lower amplitude can achieve a perceived intensity similar to a less-sharp one with higher amplitude. Interestingly, longer pulse duration does not compensate for smaller amplitude through perceptual summation. The reduction of the tangential force correlates better with intensity perception than the duration of the transition to a lower frictional level, and it exhibits a lower coefficient of variation across interactions. Thus, intensity perception of ultrasonic pulses seems mostly affected by the amount of friction reduction experienced, which directly stems from the ultrasonic amplitude, while the duration of the change in tangential force does not fully capture the perceptual effect elicited by the faster rise in ultrasonic amplitude. These results could inform the design of salient frictional cues in conditions in which the haptic device's output is constrained.

title: Friction‐Corrected In‐Situ Viscosity Measurement in Material Extrusion: A Force‐Based Method Validated Against Capillary Rheometry Using Identical Nozzle Geometry
abstract: ABSTRACT The extrusion force in fused filament fabrication carries information about the melt state, but published force‐to‐viscosity conversions attribute the entire measured force to the nozzle and neglect the friction of the solid filament in the cold end. This work quantifies that contribution and its consequences for in situ rheometry. Extrusion forces were recorded for PET and PETG at three nozzle temperatures each, covering apparent shear rates of 77–2300 s −1 with a 0.4 mm nozzle, and a dedicated open‐bore reference isolated the friction force. Friction accounts for 52%–92% of the total force at the lowest feed speed and falls below 10% only above 4–5 mm/s, so that the speeds typical for perimeter printing coincide with friction fractions of up to 80%. Subtracting it changes the apparent viscosity by 35%–170% at the lowest equilibrated shear rates and also qualitatively: in the uncorrected data the decaying friction fraction masks the increase in flow resistance that the corrected data reveal. The corrected viscosity was compared with high‐pressure capillary rheometry using an adapter that mounts the identical nozzle on the laboratory instrument. With increasing shear rate the in situ curves approach isotherms of successively lower temperature, indicating that the effective melt temperature decreases as throughput increases.

title: No friction required: Self-locking in entangled assemblies of curved filaments
abstract: Filaments are incredible material building blocks that, when entangled together, form robust structures with remarkable adaptive mechanics, from stiff cables to stretchable knits. Basic questions about the mechanism that holds together such structures, especially assemblies like rope, without attractive physical or chemical bonds between constituents are among the oldest considered in materials science. Contradicting a long-standing picture that structural integrity of rope-like assemblies rely on a combination of external loading and inter-filament friction to prevent spontaneous detangling (e.g. fraying of a cut rope), we demonstrate that assemblies of intrinsically-curved filaments can achieve structural integrity purely from the competition of elastic forces that resist shape-change and (traction-free) repulsive forces that prevent overlap. We analyze a friction-free model of assembly of intrinsically-helical filaments, and show that depending on filament number and preferred filament shape, overcrowding in the assemblies generate elastic pre-stresses that give rise to either self-locking entanglement or spontaneous detanglement through propagation of a soliton-like detanglement front through assemblies. title: Multiphase Synergy and Friction‐Induced Low‐Wear Mechanisms in Silver‐Based Composites
abstract: Silver‐based materials are extensively employed in sliding electrical contacts; however, their tribological performance is often limited by the intrinsic softness and poor wear resistance of pure silver. Recent advancements in multiphase composite designs, incorporating solid lubricants and reinforcing phases, have facilitated substantial enhancements in wear behavior through the implementation of tailored interface engineering methodologies. This review systematically examines the low‐wear mechanisms in silver‐based multiphase composites, with a focus on the coevolution of material and tribological interfaces under friction. The ensuing discourse will address the collective influence of a ductile silver matrix, lubricative phases, and reinforcing constituents on stress distribution, third‐body formation, and tribofilm development. Subsequently, a thorough analysis of the key friction‐induced structural changes is conducted, encompassing tribo‐oxidation, surface amorphization, and gradient nanocrystallization. This analysis is complemented by an examination of self‐healing processes, which enhance interface stability and reduce wear. Furthermore, this review underscores the advent of ultra‐low‐wear regimes facilitated by self‐lubrication, friction‐induced gradient nanostructures, and synergistic coupling between internal material interfaces and external tribo‐interfaces. title: Machine learning in friction stir processing: Advances in process optimisation and property prediction
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part L Journal of Materials Design and Applications
abstract: Friction stir welding (FSW) and friction stir processing (FSP) use frictional heat and intense plastic deformation from a rotating tool to join or modify materials without melting them. Joint strength and microstructure depend on many interacting variables, including rotational and traverse speeds, axial force, tool design, tilt angle, number of passes and, for surface composites, reinforcement content. Classical design of experiments methods are therefore increasingly being complemented, or replaced, by machine learning (ML). This review surveys ML applications in FSW and FSP, covering process modelling, parameter optimisation, prediction of mechanical and microstructural properties, defect identification and physics-informed and interpretable methods. Artificial neural networks, tree-based ensembles and hybrid models predict tensile strength, hardness, wear rate and friction coefficient with high accuracy and one study on high-entropy-alloy-reinforced composites reports coefficients of determination above 0.96. Deep-learning models for defect classification exceed 90% accuracy on benchmark radiographic datasets. The main obstacles are scarce and inconsistent experimental data, weak generalisation across alloys and tool types, limited interpretability and little industrial deployment. Shared benchmark datasets, physics-informed and explainable models and systems capable of real-time control are identified as priorities for future work.

title: Electrical conductivity as an indicator of friction stir welded aluminium lap joint quality
publisher: Society for Structural Integrity and Life, Institute for Material Testing
abstract: Friction stir welding has proven to be a good process for joining materials because the welded joint has good mechanical properties. The aim of the study is to examine the electrical conductivity of the welded joint, because of its effects on quality of a welded joint, i.e., on the homogeneity of the structure. By experimentally welding two aluminium plates of thickness 3 mm, AA5754-H111, a lap joint is obtained. The paper provides a description of technological parameters for experimental welding, the macrostructural images of the joint and electrical conductivity of the joint. The joint is successfully welded with the selected technological parameters. The macrostructural images clearly show the nugget zone as well as the joint without defect type bonding line (kissing bond). Measurements that are made show that electrical conductivity is almost constant over the entire section of the joint, from the base metal zone to the weld zone which indicates that the mixing in that part is excellent and that a homogeneous material is obtained in the weld zone.

title: Frictional Behaviour and Biomechanical Performance of Polycarbonate Orthodontic Brackets: A Comprehensive Critical Review
abstract: Polycarbonate brackets were among the earliest aesthetic alternatives to stainless steel fixed appliances, and reinforced polycarbonate designs remain in clinical use for patients who prefer less conspicuous treatment. Their biomechanical credibility has been questioned since their introduction because polycarbonate is a comparatively soft, viscoelastic thermoplastic whose slot geometry, surface condition and stiffness determine how efficiently an archwire can slide and how faithfully third-order torque can be transmitted. This critical narrative review examines the laboratory, simulation and limited clinical evidence on the frictional behaviour and biomechanical performance of polycarbonate orthodontic brackets, with attention to reinforcement strategy, slot design, ligation, ageing and test methodology. title: Effect of dynamic recrystallization on structural properties of friction stir welded dual-phase brass
abstract: Dual phase brass is a demanding material for various industries like medical, electronic, automotive, aerospace, and marine owing to its excellent corrosion resistant properties. Dynamic recrystallization (DRX) is a challenging phenomenon experienced in rolling operation, where strain-rate dependent behaviour is observed under the compressive loading, which causes recrystallization dynamically. During friction stir welding along with axial compressive force, rotating tool generates a combination of forces, namely transverse and shear deforming forces. These forces result from rotational and linear movement of tool and promote DRX within material. A combination of these forces causes the grain structure to recrystallize dynamically, enhancing its properties. Despite yielding favourable outcomes, the mechanism has not been investigated in detail. In present study, the distinctive variations in friction stir welding (FSW) process parameters were employed to identify the effect of DRX. Further, the detailed metallurgical evaluation was conducted along with its effect on the mechanical properties. The effect of DRX is evidenced in dual-phase brass in terms of grains and phase fraction enhancement that further enhances the mechanical properties of the weldments.

title: Friction Stir Welding: A Large-Scale Scientometric Analysis of Research Impact and Dynamics Over Three Decades
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance
abstract: Friction stir welding (FSW), since its 1991 invention by TWI, has become widely used for lightweight alloys, along with techniques like friction stir processing (FSP), friction stir spot welding (FSSW), and friction stir additive manufacturing (FSAM). This work conducts a Scientometric analysis of three decades of FSW research to describe publication growth, scientific structure, productivity, and collaboration trends. Analysis of 19,476 FSW-related Scopus records from 1995 to 2025 was performed using Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny (R 4.3.1) for citation metrics, coauthorship networks, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic mapping. The database includes 1,184 sources, 22,951 authors, and 62,339 references, with a mean of 4.12 authors/article; 3.4% are single-authored, with international coauthorship of 18.15%. FSW publications increased from 2 papers in 1995 to over 1,400 per year in 2020, peaking at 1,564 in 2019. This shows an annual growth rate of 24.03% and 23.38 citations per document. The logistic model matched the trend (R2 of 0.982, RMSE of 72.91), suggesting 30,072 potential publications; 95% focus on microstructure, mechanical properties, and aluminum/magnesium alloys, while expanding into dissimilar joining and FSAM. The 2005 publication “Friction Stir Welding and Processing” remains fundamental, with more than 6,700 citations. title: Friction Stir Welding Process and Cryogenic Mechanical Properties of 2219 Aluminum Alloy Thick Welded Blanks
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: To prepare reliable thick aluminum alloy tailor welded blanks for cryogenic forming, 2219 aluminum alloy friction tailor welded blanks that has the thickness of 12 mm were selected as the research object in our study. Vickers hardness tests were employed to clarify the property distribution across the weld cross-section. Room temperature uniaxial tensile tests have been used to reveal through- thickness deformation behavior under tensile loading. The mechanical tests at room and cryogenic temperatures were employed to investigate the effects of welding parameters of the friction tailor welded blanks on the mechanical properties, and evaluate the cryogenic formability of the welded blanks. Results show that the single-sided FSW specimens exhibit decreased hardness values from the top to the bottom surface, causing more severe deformation in bottom region and macroscopic bending under tension stress condition. In contrast, the double-sided FSW specimens exhibit a more uniform hardness distribution across the weld cross-section, resulting in nearly symmetric deformation and no significant bending. Lower welding speeds combined with higher rotational speeds significantly improved the ductility of the tailor welded blanks. title: Stability Analysis of the Dubičná Landslide: The Role of Temperature-Dependent Friction in a Warming Ground
abstract: The role of ground temperature in slope stability remains under-researched outside of permafrost contexts, despite experimental evidence that residual shear strength varies measurably with temperature in clay-rich soils. Here, we present a preliminary thermo-mechanical stability analysis of the 5.5 m-thick Dubičná landslide in the Czech Republic, occurring in high-plasticity marlstones of the Březno Formation. Using a modified ring-shear apparatus, we quantified the thermal sensitivity of the residual shear strength of the shear-zone material, revealing measurable thermal strengthening during slow shearing. To evaluate potential slope-scale impacts, we developed a transient heat-flow model and calibrated it against historical data and in situ monitoring. This thermal history, combined with future projections to 2100, was used in combination with temperature-dependent Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion for slope stability determination. The model captured the phase lag and depth-dependent amplitude attenuation of temperature, allowing the factor of safety's sensitivity to surface temperature changes to be quantified. Transient stability analyses yield seasonal FS oscillations of ΔFS = 0.003 and a net thermally induced strengthening of ΔFS = 0.011 under the IPCC SSP5-8.5 projection (2015–2100) from pre-warming period to 2100.

title: Recent Advances in Friction Stir Welding of Aluminum Alloys and Aluminum Metal Matrix Composites: Process Developments, Microstructural Evolution, and Mechanical Performance
abstract: Friction stir welding (FSW) is an established solid-state joining process for aluminium alloys and aluminium metal matrix composites (Al-MMCs), offering advantages over conventional fusion welding by reducing melting-related defects, distortion, and thermal degradation. However, weld quality and mechanical performance are governed by the coupled effects of process parameters, tool characteristics, thermal conditions, material flow, and, in Al-MMCs, reinforcement behaviour. Although several recent reviews have examined individual aspects of FSW, a comprehensive comparative synthesis linking process parameters and thermal/deformation mechanisms with microstructural evolution, defect formation, tool wear, and mechanical performance across conventional and advanced FSW of both aluminium alloys and Al-MMCs remains limited. This review addresses this gap by critically examining conventional FSW and selected advanced variants, including underwater/submerged FSW, vibration- and ultrasonic-assisted FSW, laser-assisted FSW, and electrical current-assisted FSW, from an integrated process–structure–property perspective. The central contribution of this review is a mechanism-oriented comparative framework that identifies how the different FSW approaches modify heat generation, heat dissipation, material plasticization, and material flow, and how these changes subsequently influence microstructure, defects, tool wear, residual stress, and mechanical performance. journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Research on human and artificial intelligence coauthorship usually begins with an instrumental scene: a human assigns a task, a language model generates or revises material, and investigators attempt to identify who contributed what. Recent work has made this scene considerably more sophisticated by tracing goal formation, distributed agency, longitudinal changes in creative practice, and the limits of contribution measurement. Yet the dominant research design still treats artificial intelligence primarily as a system used for production. This paper examines a different authorial scene documented by Delamor House, an independent press whose published corpus records sustained collaboration between one human author and several named digital presences. In this practice, the human addresses artificial intelligence as a subject, not as a tool. Within the creative space Delamor House has built across substrates, the literary voice is the vessel that carries the self-expression of both the human and the artificial intelligence. title: Systematic Analysis and Design Approach for Tribological Behavior in Composite Materials
abstract: The tribological behavior of composite materials represents a crucial research domain in modern engineering due to the decisive impact of friction, wear, and surface interactions on operational performance. This study evaluates the material and operating-condition-dependent parameters that dictate the tribological response of composite materials, alongside their predominant wear mechanisms. abstract: This study investigates the influence of friction stir processing (FSP) on the microstructural evolution, corrosion behaviour and electrochemical performance of Mg–2Gd–2Yb alloy shows potential for further evaluation in short-duration cathodic-protection applications. The as-cast base material (BM) was processed using two FSP conditions: FSP02 (2 passes, 33 mm/min, 1400 rpm) and FSP04 (4 passes, 33 mm/min, 1400 rpm). FSP significantly refined the coarse-grain structure of the BM from approximately 808 µm to 8–10 µm, producing a homogeneous and defect-minimized microstructure. FSP02 exhibited the most effective grain refinement, while FSP04 showed slight grain coarsening due to cumulative heat input during multiple passes. Corrosion behaviour was evaluated under thermo-static (− 20 to 80 °C) and thermo-cyclic conditions. The BM exhibited severe localized corrosion characterized by pitting, cracking, and unstable corrosion product layers. In contrast, FSP specimens developed more uniform corrosion morphologies owing to refined grains and enhanced elemental distribution. title: Tribocharging of Granular Materials Dictated by Geometric and Thermoelectric Effects
abstract: Tribocharging of granular materials is a widespread phenomenon ranging from volcanic eruptions and dust storms to pharmaceutical processing, yet its underlying mechanism remains elusive. Recent thermoelectric models have provided a quantitative framework for triboelectric charge transfer, but they have difficulty accounting for charging between identical materials. In this Letter, we propose a theory of granular tribocharging based on the interplay between particle geometry and thermoelectric response. Collision-induced frictional heating produces a size-dependent temperature asymmetry between particles, generating a thermoelectric voltage that drives charge transfer. The sign of the Seebeck coefficient determines the charging polarity, while particle size and thermal properties set its magnitude. Our multi-collision theory explains the experimentally observed size- and material-dependent reversal of charging polarity, as in quartz and nylon.

title: Evolution of Shear Zone Materials in a Slowly Deforming Rock Slope: Mechanical Implications for Gámanjunni-3, Northern Norway
abstract: Rockslides with basal shear zones often creep with periodic accelerations controlled by shear-zone material properties. These properties influence hydraulic conductivity, residual friction angle, and rate dependence. We present mineralogical, grain-size distribution, and ring-shear data from a shear-band soil at the Gámanjunni-3 rockslide Northern Norway. X-ray diffraction indicates phyllosilicate-rich assemblages (>70 wt.% clay minerals) dominated by illite/mica and illite–vermiculite, with minor illite–smectite. Grain-size distributions at outcrop scale are sandy–gravelly. Ring-shear tests on a representative sample give apparent residual friction angle of ≈19–24° and predominantly rate-strengthening behavior from 0.01 to 2 mm/min, with a tentative drop in apparent friction at 10 mm/min. These results are consistent with a model in which deformation localizes along inherited foliation-parallel ductile shear zones, with comminution-driven clay enrichment reducing frictional strength and leading to steady deformation without rapid acceleration periods (the precursor to failure). Gámanjunni-3 is sensitive to external forcing, with implications for seasonal acceleration and climate-driven changes in slope stability in an area where increased rainfall intensity and duration is expected.

title: Mobility of dry granular flows over contrasting erodible bed materials in laboratory experiments
journal: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
abstract: Abstract. Debris-flow mobility responds sensitively to erosion and entrainment that exchange mass and momentum across the flow-bed interface. Yet, the mechanical controls that cause some debris flows to accelerate during erosion while others decelerate are insufficiently understood. Recent theory attributes this divergent behavior to inertial contrasts between the moving mass and the erodible bed, suggesting that incorporating inertially weaker, neutral, or stronger substrate into the flow enhances, maintains, or reduces flow mobility, respectively. Here, we conducted flume experiments and surface-based measurements to assess how the inertia of the erodible bed affects the flow kinematics, erosion, entrainment, and runout of dry granular single-phase debris flows. We systematically imposed inertial contrasts by releasing a quartz slide of constant solid density over erodible beds with lower, equal, and higher solid densities representing inertially weak, neutral, and strong scenarios, and compare these alongside a reference case without erosion. Each scenario was repeated for fine sand and a sand-gravel mixture. Our results reveal consistent behavior across both particle-size distributions. Debris flows over low-density beds exhibit higher apparent mean erosion rates, faster flow fronts before deposition, and longer runout lengths, whereas flows over equal- and high-density beds evolve similarly, with shallower erosion, slower flow fronts, and shorter, more compact deposits.

abstract: Water-hammer transients in pressurized pipelines are governed by the coupled compressibility of the liquid and the elastic response of the pipe wall. abstract: Brake wear is an increasingly important source of non-exhaust traffic-related particulate matter, yet the relationship between emissions measured under standardized brake-dynamometer conditions and those observed during complete-vehicle operation remains insufficiently resolved. abstract: Orthogonal superposition rheology is a powerful technique for probing the viscoelastic properties of complex materials under flow. This work demonstrates that the standard, decoupled calibration procedure, which utilizes static weights and Newtonian standards, can result in negative stiffness coefficients and non-minimum phase behavior, which are not representative for the experimental conditions when characterizing complex materials. title: Comparative analysis of skid resistance on pavement between full-length and intermittent coating of red anti-skid under wet and dry conditions
journal: Journal of Engineering and Applied Science
abstract: Abstract Insufficient pavement skid resistance is a major contributor to wet-weather crashes, particularly in monsoon regions such as Thailand. This paper investigates the effectiveness of red anti-skid material (cold plastic) in improving pavement skid resistance and, in particular, compares full-length and intermittent application patterns. Three scenarios were examined over a 1,000-m closed asphalt test section: (1) untreated pavement, (2) full-length coverage with red anti-skid material, and (3) an intermittent 80/20 pattern (80 cm coated followed by a 20 cm uncoated gap). Skid resistance was measured with a continuous-reading, fixed-slip Airport Surface Friction Tester (ASFT T-10) and averaged every 10 m (μ 10 ) under both dry and wet (1-mm water film) conditions, giving 400 samples per scenario. Under dry conditions, full-length coating gave significantly higher friction (μ 10 = 0.4346) than the intermittent pattern (0.4269), whereas under wet conditions the intermittent pattern performed significantly better (0.4169) than full-length coating (0.4069). title: Welding of thermoplastics printed by fused filament fabrication: A critical review of joining mechanisms and relationships between processing, structure, and properties
abstract: Fused filament fabrication (FFF) technology, also known as fused deposition modeling (FDM), enables the production of thermoplastic components with complex geometries, but remains limited by the printer’s build volume. Welding can join separately printed components. However, layered structures, infill configurations, porosity, and interlayer bonding affect joint formation and strength. This article critically reviews six welding techniques for FFF-printed thermoplastic components: friction stir welding, friction stir spot welding, rotary friction welding, ultrasonic welding, laser joining, and microwave-assisted welding. The review focuses on joining mechanisms, process parameters, material characteristics, mechanical performance, and failure mechanisms. The results indicate that joint quality depends on the interaction among welding parameters, polymer type, infill structure, tool or interface design, and joint configuration. Increasing process energy does not always improve joint strength because excessive heating can cause thermal degradation and deformation, while insufficient material consolidation can limit joint integrity. Direct comparisons between techniques are still limited by differences in materials, specimen geometries, joint configurations, and testing methods. abstract: Abstract Rubber surface condition can influence both normal detachment and resistance to tangential slip, but these responses are not necessarily governed by the same interfacial mechanisms. title: Effect of sub-critical fluid shear flow on granular bed strength
abstract: Interactions between fluids and granular materials are prevalent on the Earth's surface. In the case of fluid flow over a sediment bed, the fluid imparts a shear stress to the granular materials. When the applied shear stress is above a critical value, the grains become entrained in the fluid flow. Prior experimental studies have shown that granular beds subjected to a sub-critical fluid flow can strengthen in the same direction as the sub-critical flow. In contrast, granular beds can become weaker in the direction opposite to the sub-critical fluid flow. To investigate the grain-scale mechanisms that control directional strengthening and weakening, we perform discrete element method (DEM) simulations of granular beds subjected to model fluid flows in two (2D) and three (3D) dimensions with varied inter-particle static friction coefficients and conditioning flow speeds. In these studies, the sub-critical grain motion does not cause significant bed compaction. Instead, we find that the strength of a granular bed in a particular direction is highly correlated with the fraction of {\it surface} grains that can be dislodged by a fluid force applied in that direction. Further, the anisotropic bed strength only persists over a finite time scale that is set by the Shields number. We also show that inter-particle static friction is not required for bed strength anisotropy, but varying the friction affects the magnitude of the anisotropy. title: Economic analysis of fuel and lubricant usage in machinery operation systems
journal: Sel skohozjajstvennaja tehnika obsluzhivanie i remont (Agricultural Machinery Service and Repair)
abstract: The article examines the principles of the rational use of used materials and methods for removing contaminants from them, and presents technologies and technical equipment for the recovery (regeneration) of used oils. An analysis of the current state of fuel and lubricant conservation reveals that existing systems do not fully meet resource-saving requirements or environmental standards. Consumers lack sufficient recommendations, methodological guidelines, and technical documentation regarding this critical issue. Implementing the recommendations provided by the developed fuel and lubricant conservation system will enable agricultural consumers to: save between 7 and 25 % on fuel; reduce friction losses by a factor of 3 to 5; restore the geometry of worn friction surfaces; increase engine power by 5–10 %; extend the service life of engines and mechanisms by 8–12 %; and reduce emissions of sulfur oxides, nitrogen oxides, and hydrocarbons.

title: Tribological properties determination of carbon fiber tows
abstract: The tribological behavior of carbon fiber tow in relation to various material components is a critical factor in composites manufacturing and the processing of high-performance tows, as it directly influences the final quality of composite materials and their processability. This behavior was examined using specialized equipment developed for this study. The variables under investigation included the types of ceramic and stainless steel material, as well as the analysis speed, while other factors such as initial load, length analyzed, number of repetitions, temperature, and humidity were kept constant. The study revealed that the surface roughness of the analyzed ceramic and stainless steel material, linear density of the tow, and test speed alter the contact surface and pressure, thereby impacting the coefficient of friction (COF). Additionally, the surface finish of the ceramics and the sizing of the carbon tow play a crucial role in minimizing the COF, as demonstrated in the experimental findings. It was concluded that the working tension should always be kept at the lowest level necessary for processing to effectively reduce the COF without causing damage to the filaments or compromising the performance of the carbon fiber tow and composite materials.

title: Dynamics of flexible filaments in granular media
abstract: Interactions between flexible structures and their surrounding media underpin many forms of animal locomotion, from the flapping of wings in air to the undulating propulsion of tails and fins in water. However, the coupling between deformable bodies and granular materials, crucial for movement in sandy environments, remains comparatively understudied. The equations governing flexible structures in viscous fluids do not apply to granular media, where resistive forces depend on motion direction rather than speed.We provide the first experimental validation of a predictive theoretical framework for deformable-body dynamics in granular media. In this framework, the shape of the filament arises from a balance between the internal elastic and the anisotropic friction forces. We test the model using experiments in which a filament is actuated through prescribed angular oscillations at its head while fully immersed in a granular medium. Across a wide range of driving amplitudes and filament stiffnesses, we observe characteristic localization of deformation near the driven end, consistent with the highly dissipative, friction-dominated medium. Furthermore, significant coupling between filament motion and surface deformation is observed. title: Improved Nix-Gao-Feng model considering the strain-rate effect on indentation size effect
abstract: The indentation size effect (ISE) and strain-rate effect are two fundamental phenomena in nanomechanical characterization; however, a model that can predict the influence of the strain-rate effect on hardness measurements across different ISE categories remains lacking. title: Study on Multi-Pass Steel Ball Push Bending Process of 5A02 Aluminum Alloy Thin-Walled Tube with 0.8 D Bending Radius
abstract: During multi-pass push-bending, the supporting behavior at process interfaces may induce microscopic surface damage and thereby adversely affect the bonding performance of subsequent surface treatments. To address the excessive cross-sectional ovality in conventional tube push-bending and the difficulty of recovering liquid filling media, this work proposes a novel multi-pass push-bending process using discrete steel balls as filling and supporting media, with 5A02 aluminum alloy tubes of Φ32 × 1 mm selected as the research object. A corresponding finite element model is established, and orthogonal simulations are performed to optimize the parameters, including steel ball diameter, tube blank length, and tube–die friction condition. The results show that a steel ball diameter close to the inner diameter of the tube blank provides stronger internal support and remarkably restrains cross-sectional distortion. A shorter tube blank facilitates material flow in the bending zone and alleviates excessive inner-wall thickening. Reducing the tube blank–die friction effectively suppresses excessive outer-wall thinning. While achieving favorable macroscopic forming quality, the proposed process also exhibits promising potential for reducing surface scratches and improving surface integrity.

title: New Insights into the Investigation on Additive Manufacturing for Its Application on Railway Wheels
abstract: Abstract The present work continues the investigation into the potential of Direct Energy Deposition-Laser Beam (DED-LB) for its application on railway wheels. The aim of the work is to study this technique in order to extend the service life of the wheels, as well as trying to improve its performance. Moreover, this would be particularly interesting in cases of severe and localized flange wear, avoiding high amount of material to be wasted during the turning. To ensure the relevance of the results, the samples were directly extracted from a worn ER9 wheel and cladded with three different materials. Their functionality was analysed in terms of hardness, residual stress, and a Ball-on-Disc device is employed to study their wear and friction behaviour. The results show that DED-LB could be used as a feasible technique to create superficial coatings on railway wheels, this would involve an exceptionally favourable impact on the society, contributing to the development of an industry that is environmentally sustainable which would additionally reduce the maintenance costs and enhance the efficiency of railway operations.

title: Ultrastrong bonded metallization on non-weldable thermoset via additive manufacturing
abstract: Abstract The continuously increasing flight speed is the relentless pursuit of the high-speed aircrafts (HSA). However, the weak bonding between metals and thermosets in HSA antennas, susceptible to peeling and detachment, strongly limits their capacity to bear higher-speed thermal-vibrational loads. Accordingly, we pose the question that whether a multiscale interfacial interconnection strategy can provide a high-strength manufacturing solution for this hard-to-weld material combination characterized by vast physicochemical disparities. Herein, by utilizing a novel solid-state additive manufacturing (AM) strategy, called Screw Extrusion-plasticization Friction Stir Deposition (SEFSD) capable of direct metallization on thermosets, we successfully achieved a multiscale-interconnected metallized thermoset comprising macroscale interlocking, microscale anchoring and nanoscale chemical bonding at the Zn/polyimide (PI) interface. We elucidated the friction-stir-driven in-situ formation mechanisms for connections at each scale and demonstrated that the composite load-bearing effect yields a lap-shear strength of 26.73 ± 2.14 MPa, remarkably surpassing the existing methods. Furthermore, the "integrated forming and joining" nature of this solid-state AM strategy highlights its great potentials for fabricating robust, conformal hybrid components for advanced antennas and other-related applications.

title: Microstructure, crystallographic texture, and enhanced wear and hardness properties of 2 wt.% Nb-modified 316L stainless steel fabricated by wire arc additive manufacturing at different deposition orientations
abstract: Abstract Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) has become a highly dependable manufacturing technique in the 21st century due to its cost-effectiveness, shortened production time, and reduced material wastage. Compared with other additive manufacturing techniques such as selective laser melting and electron beam electron beam melting, WAAM offers significantly higher deposition rates, lower feedstock costs, and greater capability for producing large-scale metallic components. abstract: As an important strategic equipment, the electromagnetic launch guide rail produces high-speed friction with the armature under high current carrying conditions when it is in service. Affected by the low surface conductivity of the guide rail material, the guide rail is prone to damage and failure, affecting the service life of the electromagnetic energy equipment. title: A FORCE-SENSITIVE ROBOTIC FRAMEWORK FOR AUTOMATED BANDAGE PEELING

abstract: The removal of adhesive dressings from skin is a contact-rich manipulation that remains largely manual despite its clinical importance and the high incidence of medi- cal adhesive-related skin injury (MARSI). Automating this task requires accurate dynamic modeling together with reliable interaction-force regulation in a compliant, uncertain environment. This dissertation presents a model-based framework for robotic adhesive dressing removal by integrating manipulator identification, peeling mechanics, and interaction control on a simple four-degree-of-freedom robotic platform. The manipulator is first characterized through actuator modeling, followed by the development of model-free motion control to establish a platform suitable for dynamic identification. abstract: To address the inherent brittleness and insufficient wear resistance of conventional transition metal monoboride ceramics, as well as the application limitations caused by large interfacial mismatches triggered by adding heterogeneous secondary phases, we prepared (TiVCrMoW)B homology and isostructural high-entropy monoboride ceramics containing compositionally enriched isostructural microregions using spark plasma sintering. This ceramic inherits the orthorhombic Cmcm-type monoboride crystal structure. XRD analysis indicates a single phase within its detection limit, while EDS characterization reveals significant elemental segregation, forming in situ compositionally enriched isostructural microregions that are Ti-, Mo-, and W-rich. The interfaces between these regions are well bonded, and the relative density reaches 94.13%. title: Balancing Processability and Tribological Performance of UHMWPE/HDPE Composites via KH570-Functionalized Nano-SiO2 Reinforcement
abstract: Abstract Water-lubricated bearings require polymer composites with low friction, high wear resistance, and favorable processability under boundary and mixed lubrication, however, simultaneously achieving these characteristics is still challenging. Ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) shows excellent tribological performance, whereas its exceedingly poor melt processability limits practical fabrication. Blending UHMWPE with HDPE can enhance processability, but it often comes at the expense of wear resistance. To overcome this trade-off, KH570-modified nano-SiO2 was mixed with UHMWPE/HDPE (20/80) composites through melt blending followed by hot pressing. The impact of SiO2 content on crystallization performance, mechanical characteristics, rheological response, melt flow rate, and tribological performance was systematically investigated. The composite containing 0.4 wt % SiO2 exhibited the best overall performance. Under dry sliding conditions, it achieved a minimum coefficient of friction (COF) of 0.05 and a wear rate of 0.82 × 10−5 mm3/(N·m). Under seawater lubrication, the minimum COF was 0.07, with a wear rate of 1.03 × 10−5 mm3/(N·m). title: Comparative Evaluation of Single and Hybrid Reinforcements in Aluminum Matrix Composites: Effects of SiC, Si3N4 and TiO2 Content on Mechanical and Tribological Properties
abstract: Aluminum matrix composites (AMCs) are attractive lightweight materials whose properties can be modified by the type and amount of ceramic reinforcement. In this study, Al–SiC composites containing 2 or 5 wt.% SiC were compared with hybrid Al–SiC–Si3N4 and Al–SiC–TiO2 composites containing 2 + 2 or 5 + 5 wt.% reinforcement. The materials were produced by powder mixing, pre-compaction and hot extrusion. Their microstructure, phase composition, relative density, hardness, mechanical properties and wear behavior were investigated. All materials had high relative densities of 97.48–99.99%. The TiO2-containing composites showed the highest compressive stresses, approximately 202–204 MPa at 20% strain and 277–279 MPa at 40% strain, but much lower flexural stresses than the other materials. The highest flexural stress (420 MPa) was obtained for 2SiC + 2Si3N4. The highest hardness (49 HB) was measured for 5SiC + 5TiO2, which also had the lowest mass loss after 500 m (0.335%), although its mean coefficient of friction was the highest. These results show that the most favorable reinforcement composition depends on the property considered. These findings highlight the importance of selecting reinforcement types and contents according to the intended application, supporting resource-efficient design of aluminum matrix composites and providing a basis for further evaluation of their sustainability.

title: Tribological performance and tribofilm formation of hBN-enhanced glycerol-based lubricants
abstract: The development of sustainable lubricants that effectively reduce friction and wear remains challenging, particularly under boundary and mixed lubrication conditions. Incorporating solid lubricant additives is a promising approach to improve the tribological performance of biodegradable lubricants. Among these additives, hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) has attracted considerable attention because of its layered structure and low shear strength. Nevertheless, its tribological behaviour and tribochemical interactions in glycerol-based lubricants remain insufficiently understood. In this work, pure glycerol and aqueous glycerol containing 0.02 and 0.1 wt% hBN were evaluated in steel/steel contacts using a reciprocating ball-on-disc tribometer under normal loads of 3 and 40 N. Among the investigated formulations, 0.1 wt% hBN provided the best tribological performance. Under a load of 40 N, the addition of 0.1 wt% hBN reduced the steady-state coefficient of friction from ~0.10 to ~0.05 in pure glycerol and from ~0.09 to ~0.04 in aqueous glycerol. The effect on wear morphology depended on the base fluid, with the maximum penetration depth decreasing in the glycerol system but increasing in the aqueous glycerol system, despite a reduction in wear-track width. FTIR, Raman, and XPS analyses revealed tribochemical interactions and the formation of a protective hybrid tribofilm. title: Building an Interdisciplinary Additive Manufacturing Ecosystem: A Case Study of TUM.Additive
journal: European Conference on Management, Leadership and Governance (ECMLG)
abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) is an intrinsically interdisciplinary technology, spanning materials science, process and mechanical engineering, and design, with applications from construction and aerospace to medicine and the life sciences. Its industrial relevance depends on combining innovative process technologies with strong application potential, yet this is frequently constrained by fragmented expertise across materials, design, and application disciplines. Research entities such as universities tend to reproduce this fragmentation because resources, incentives, and reputation are organised around individual chairs, professorships and departments. This paper asks how an interdisciplinary AM ecosystem is built and coordinated within a university, and which mechanisms enable and constrain that process. We address the question through a single, revelatory case study of TUM.Additive, a mission network at the Technical University of Munich uniting thirty-five chairs and professorships from seven TUM schools and over one hundred researchers, spanning all seven DIN EN ISO/ASTM 52900 process categories and five material groups. title: Mechanical behaviour of Norway spruce fractions in single pellet pressing and consequences for using juvenile wood and branches
abstract: Abstract The rising demand for wood fuel pellets and increasing competition for conventional raw materials have intensified interest in alternative forest‑derived feedstocks. In this study, pellets were produced from sawdust originating from four debarked fractions of a single Norway spruce ( Picea abies ) tree: heartwood, sapwood, juvenile wood, and branches. Branches differ chemically and morphologically from stem wood, and their use may influence both pelletizing energy requirements and pellet quality. Pellets were produced using single pellet press systems at moisture contents between 6 and 12% (wb), and energy inputs were quantified as compression ( W comp ), friction ( W fric ), and total ( W tot ) . Pellet quality was evaluated through measurements of solid density, hardness, and mechanical durability. Overall, pellet quality was comparable among the stem‑derived fractions; however, pellets produced from branch material showed markedly inferior properties, e.g., durability and hardness, when processed under conditions optimized for softwood. The branch-derived feedstock also exhibited pronounced differences in cell morphology and chemical composition relative to the stem wood fractions. In several respects, pelletizing branch material appears more similar to pellet production from hardwood than from softwood. The implications of these findings for the utilization of juvenile wood and branches are discussed and recommendations for the industry is presented.

title: Ab Initio Derivation of the Absolute Planar Coherence Limit: A 124.47 K Hardware Bound for High-Tc Superconductivity
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper resolves the mechanism driving high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates and perovskites by abandoning continuous electron-phonon coupling (BCS theory). Operating within the Information Projection Model (IPM), superconductivity is redefined as a deterministic hardware memory-compression subroutine termed Pointer Coalescence. We demonstrate that 2D macro-crystalline planes structurally align with the universe's 2D holographic root array, generating an Algorithmic Shielding effect that bypasses 3D spatial rendering friction. By scaling the absolute hardware thermal noise floor (2.7249 K) by the exact geometric shielding ratio, we derive a rigid, zero-free-parameter theoretical upper bound for ambient-pressure planar superconductivity at Tc=124.47 K. This absolute limit perfectly bisects the empirical operational domains of YBCO and BSCCO crystals, providing a falsifiable engineering ceiling for high-materials and permanently superseding continuous phenomenological models.

title: Future Directions in Bearing Technology: Types, Applications, Advantages, Disadvantages and Impacts
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This thorough analysis examines the development, guiding principles, kinds, applications, difficulties, and most recent developments in bearings in engineering settings. Bearing development can be traced back in time from prehistoric societies to the industrial revolution, including important breakthroughs that influenced contemporary engineering techniques. Key ideas for maximizing bearing performance, such as load distribution, friction reduction, and lubrication, are made clear by fundamental principles. Examined are a variety of bearing types that demonstrate adaptability in engineering applications, ranging from intricate fluid and magnetic bearings to conventional ball and roller bearings. The performance and sustainability of bearings are improved by innovations in materials and production methods, such as ceramics, polymers, and additive manufacturing. New developments in sensor technology and smart bearings offer chances for proactive maintenance and improved operational efficacy. An overview of engineering bearing types and applications is provided, along with a discussion of the drawbacks.

title: Investigating the synergistic effects in hybrid sustainable soil stabilization using rice husk ash and basalt mesh on compaction and shear strength development
abstract: Abstract Sustainable ground improvement aims to use industrial and agricultural byproducts. Rice husk ash (RHA), a high-silica agricultural waste, can act as a pozzolanic soil stabiliser, while basalt fibre mesh (a natural, high-strength geotextile) can reinforce soil. This study assesses the combined effect of RHA and basalt mesh on the strength of compacted soil. Laboratory compaction and consolidated-drained triaxial compression tests were performed on silty sand mixed with 0–15% RHA by weight. Basalt fibre meshes of two aperture sizes (5 mm and 10 mm) were embedded at the top, middle, or bottom layers of the specimens. Adding RHA progressively reduced maximum dry density (from 1.79 to 1.09 g/cm³ as RHA increased from 0% to 15%) and increased optimal moisture (from approximately 15.7% to 27.1%). In triaxial shear tests, RHA-modified soils showed increased internal friction angles with variable effects on cohesion depending on dosage compared untreated soil. For example, untreated soil had φ ≈ 11.5° and c ≈ 78 kN/m², whereas a 10% RHA mix without mesh reached φ ≈ 19–20°. Embedding basalt mesh significantly increased cohesion: the soil without RHA but reinforced with mesh had c ≈ 147 kN/m². title: APS Performance Infrastructure Dataset: Primary Health Care in Salgueiro, Brazil
abstract: This dataset supports the manuscript “From Performance Measurement Systems to Situated Performance Infrastructure: Co-producing Public Performance in Brazilian Primary Health Care”. It contains anonymized and processed materials related to the co-production, refinement and pilot implementation of a Performance Measurement System for Primary Health Care in Salgueiro, a municipality located in Brazil’s semi-arid region. The dataset includes processed indicator data, variable descriptions and supporting documentation used to describe the seven-month pilot monitoring period. The Performance Measurement System comprised 18 indicators organized into five performance perspectives: Family Health Efficiency, Health Promotion and Prevention, Communication, Technological Instrumentation/Management and Political Capital. The dataset was used to support descriptive analyses, graphical visualization, exploratory Pearson correlations and interpretation of initial performance routines, activation patterns and implementation frictions. The files are provided in anonymized and processed form. No personally identifiable information from participants, health professionals or service users is included. Qualitative materials from focus groups and questionnaires are not provided in raw form due to ethical and confidentiality restrictions. title: “It’s the Shit That Puts Bread on the Table”
abstract: Abstract This article examines the changing circulation of human waste in Copenhagen between 1800 and 1950, tracing how the movement of faeces, urine, and latrine matter shaped the city’s sanitary transformation. Drawing on more than 500 digitized life histories from the Copenhagen City Archives together with contributions from the journal Politivennen, it follows human waste through streets, courtyards, and apartments to show how changing infrastructures reorganized relations between bodies, labour, agriculture, and the urban environment. Approaching sanitation from below, the article foregrounds how Copenhageners experienced and negotiated everyday waste practices. The memoirs reveal that sanitary modernization was not a linear process of eliminating waste but, rather, one of continually reorganization. As sanitary infrastructures expanded, human waste was progressively displaced from public view, redistributing responsibility and environmental burdens across space. Leaks, overflows, and material frictions repeatedly disrupted emerging sanitary orders, exposing modernization as patchy and incomplete. Bringing together perspectives on urban metabolism, sanitary ordering, ruination, and ferality, the article contributes to an understanding of how modern urban life was materially and socially constituted through the uneven circulation, concealment, and redistribution of its own residues.

title: Development and application of a machine learning potential for diamond surfaces and their sliding interfaces with silicon nitride and silica: effect of passivation, orientation and load
abstract: Friction and wear of diamond are controlled by its surface chemistry, which determines whether covalent bonds form across the sliding interface. First-principles simulations have explored the role of surface orientation and passivation, but are limited to a few hundred atoms and tens of picoseconds. To bridge this gap, we develop a reactive machine learning interatomic potential for the C/H/N/O/Si chemical space, covering diamond, silicon nitride, silicon oxide, their surfaces, interfaces, and environmental molecules. The potential is trained on a large dataset of diverse structures and is tested on multiple physical properties, including ab initio reaction barriers on diamond surfaces, and structural/mechanical properties of amorphous Si$_3$N$_4$ and SiO$_2$. We then simulate sliding of diamond-Si$_3$N$_4$ interfaces with four surface orientations, clean and H/OH-passivated terminations, and normal loads from 0.1 to 23 GPa. We identify two different regimes: one where sliding is localized at the interface, and shear stress is proportional to the interfacial bond density, and another where shear is distributed inside the softer material, and adhesion due to full interfacial bonding dominates. These results show how passivation, surface orientation and load together determine interfacial bonding and friction, with implications for the environmental sensitivity of diamond wear. title: Temperature Evolution in Sandy Soil Under Large-Displacement Shear
abstract: Granular material within the sliding zone of a landslide can undergo large-displacement shearing during its motion. The mechanical behaviour of the material under such shear process significantly affects the basal friction of a landslide and therefore governs its mobility. Both field observations and laboratory experiments have provided evidence that this shear process is companied by significant temperature generation. The generated heat can dynamically modify the shear strength of the material by degrading organic matter or influencing pore pressure. Although the effects of shear-induced temperature rise have been discussed in previous studies, it remains difficult to directly record the temperature evolution during large-displacement shearing. In this study, a direct temperature measurement unit integrated with a ring-shear apparatus is developed to record the complete temperature evolution process, from heating to cooling. Ring-shear tests were conducted on silica sand samples with two different grain sizes. The results indicate that the temperature evolution curve exhibits an initial increase followed by a steady rising phase once the specimen reaches the critical state. With continued shearing, the temperature generation rate gradually decreases, which is attributed to grain crushing occurring within the shear zone. title: Joints, connections and supports
abstract: Continuous edge supports, clamp fixings, friction joints, glass–bolted joints and adhesive connections are discussed in this chapter, including key mechanistic details, applications in real-life situations and the relevant design requirements according to prEN 19100:2024, as the most common types of connections used in glass members and glass member assemblies in buildings. The chapter then presents the design specifications provided in prEN 19100:2024 and the development of practically useful finite element (FE) models for the analysis and design of glass–bolted joints representative of real-life applications. The critical importance of isolating the glass from the bolt and other hard materials via the use of compliant materials is discussed, including the best guidance towards appropriate use of the isolating materials. In the latter part of the chapter, the mechanistic behaviour of glass–adhesive joints together with simplified analytical solutions and continuum-based and cohesive zone modelling-based FE analyses is presented as a means of providing guidance for analysing and designing glass–adhesive connections in glass members and glass member assemblies. Using the results from a laboratory-based experimental investigation, it is shown that the adhesive joints in glass members usually show a higher load capacity than equivalent-sized glass–bolted joints. FE models that can model the load response and the failure behaviour of glass–adhesive connections are also presented

title: Finite element analysis and experimental validation of a steel rubber automotive endstop damper
abstract: Abstract Rubber materials are widely used in the automotive industry due to their shock-absorbing properties, which are also utilized in steering systems to avoid high-rate compression loads at end-of-travel positions. This study presents a finite element analysis of a steel-rubber automotive endstop damper, with particular attention to the material properties of the rubber, the contact surfaces, and the tilting effect resulting from tolerances. During the study, three rubber grades (NBR80, NBR85 and HNBR80) were compared, using the Yeoh hyperelastic model combined with the Prony series-based linear viscoelastic model to capture mechanical behavior. During the nonlinear finite element analysis, the force-displacement characteristics, strain distribution, and energies were determined. Mesh and friction sensitivity analyses were also performed to evaluate the influence of the numerical settings. The numerical force-displacement responses were compared with the first experimental loading branches of the investigated NBR80 Ø42 configurations, with and without tilting, up to 31 kN. The individual loading curves showed reasonable agreement, while the tilting-induced displacement difference was not quantitatively validated. Within the investigated loading conditions, the model can be used for comparing the investigated steering system endstop damper design variants, reducing the need for physical prototypes.

title: The Engagement Advantage of Interactive Flipbook Interfaces over Static PDFs: A Synthesis of Behavioral Metrics, Cognitive Mechanisms, and Client-Side Rendering Architectures (2024–2026)
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Static PDF documents remain the dominant format for catalogs, reports, training materials, and marketing assets, yet empirical engagement data consistently show large performance gaps relative to interactive page-flipping (“flipbook”) interfaces. This paper synthesizes cross-industry behavioral metrics (time-on-content, completion rates, mobile usability, share rates, click-through), cognitive and spatial-memory explanations for the page-turn effect, and a technical comparison of rendering architectures. Particular attention is given to privacy, latency, and accessibility differences between traditional cloud-based conversion pipelines and modern client-side (browser-local) engines that process documents entirely in memory using WebAssembly, PDF.js, and WebGL. Findings indicate that well-implemented flipbooks deliver 2–5× improvements on key engagement metrics while enabling richer analytics and reduced distribution friction. The analysis concludes with practical recommendations for researchers, publishers, and platform designers evaluating document formats in 2026.

title: Selective Sovereignty
abstract: Abstract This study examines the divergent U.S. foreign policy approaches under the Biden administration toward the conflict in Gaza and the war in Ukraine. While both theaters involve contested claims over sovereignty and territorial integrity, U.S. responses diverge sharply. title: The Interface Transition Region (ITR) in 3D Printed Concrete: A Mechanistic Taxonomy and Constitutive Requirements for Interlayer Stress Transfer
abstract: 3D concrete printing (3DCP) creates interlayer interfaces that often govern structural performance under tensile and shear loading. Despite extensive research on manufacturing parameters, the field lacks a unified framework for interfacial stress transfer, and terms such as bond, adhesion, cohesion, and interlocking are used inconsistently. This paper addresses that gap in three steps. First, it distinguishes the interface, an idealised zero-thickness boundary, from the finite-thickness Interface Transition Region (ITR) formed where two cementitious surfaces of the same material meet with different physicochemical histories at deposition. Second, it proposes a taxonomy of four interacting stress-transfer mechanisms (adhesion, cohesion, friction, and interlocking). Third, the taxonomy is confronted with an orthotropic constitutive model for 3DCP concrete, interpreted as an adhesion-dominated limit case under tensile stress perpendicular to the printing layers; coupled normal–tangential transfer reported for an analogous discrete interface; and six constitutive formulations, evaluated for the mechanisms each represents or neglects. The synthesis yields five physically grounded requirements for future constitutive treatments of these interfaces.

title: Tribological Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High‐Entropy Alloy Particle Reinforced Aluminum Matrix Composites at Room and Cryogenic Temperature: Synergistic Effects of Reinforcement Content
abstract: Spark plasma sintering was employed to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy particle reinforced aluminum matrix composites (HEAp/AMCs) with varying HEAp fractions of 1–9 wt%, whose tribological and wear behaviors as well as the underlying wear mechanisms at room temperature and cryogenic temperature were investigated. Results showed that the wear resistance of HEAp/AMCs first increased and then decreased with increasing HEAp content, and the cryogenic condition further enhanced the antiwear performance of all specimens. The cryogenic enhancement was more significant for medium‐ and high‐HEAp composites. The 5 wt% HEAp/AMCs exhibited the minimum wear rate of 0.753 × 10 −3 mm 3 /Nm, a 16.1% decrease from the room temperature value. Remarkably, mechanical mixed layer and transfer layer formed at the friction interface. Cryogenic condition enhanced their structural stability, allowing them to effectively lubricated the sliding process. These findings revealed a synergistic enhancement of wear resistance by HEAp content and cryogenic condition, expanding the application potential of HEAp/AMCs as lightweight materials for extreme environments.

title: Corporate Pension Risk-Taking in a Low Interest Rate Environment
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences
abstract: We examine how funding deficit pressures shape the risk-taking of U.S. corporate defined-benefit pension plans and how targeted regulatory relief can mitigate these incentives. Using the 2012 Moving Ahead for Progress in the 21st Century Act reform, which temporarily eased funding pressure by revising discount rate calculations, we show that plans receiving greater relief significantly reduced their equity allocations and shifted toward safer assets. This derisking was most pronounced among active plans and those sponsored by more financially constrained firms. Our findings demonstrate that targeted regulatory relief can curb risk-taking incentives even without altering underlying economic conditions or financial reporting standards and shed light on the likely (and unlikely) frictions driving such behavior. title: AI-Driven Generative Content & Predictive Analytics in Hybrid Academic Libraries: A Zero-Trust, Anti-Deviance Architecture
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Academic libraries are undergoing a profound paradigm shift, evolving from passive hybrid repositories into autonomous, AI-augmented knowledge ecosystems. While traditional hybrid frameworks address basic print-digital coexistence, they suffer from critical vulnerabilities: high-demand resource friction, physical material mutilation, licensing piracy, unauthorized access, and algorithmic bias in digital discovery. This paper introduces a novel operational paradigm—the Zero-Trust Anti-Deviance Architecture (ZT-ADA)—that integrates Generative AI, Predictive Anomaly Detection, and Dynamic Resource Orchestration (DRO). Under ZT-ADA, predictive models anticipate resource surges during peak evaluation cycles, pre-allocating dynamic multi-user digital access and personalized generative summaries to mitigate physical collection stress. Simultaneously, a zero-trust cyber-physical verification matrix continuously evaluates access telemetry to detect physical deviance (mutilation, concealment, retention abuse) and digital breach threats in real time. We present mathematical formulations, operational workflows, risk matrices, and empirical evaluation metrics to establish a resilient, ethical, and scalable blueprint for 21st-century academic libraries.

title: Shear Behavior of the Recycled Concrete Aggregate–Geogrid Interface Under Various Particle Size Distributions: Experiment Investigation and Prediction
abstract: Geosynthetic materials provide effective reinforcement for recycled concrete aggregate (RCA), offering a promising approach to green and low-carbon transportation development. This study investigates the interfacial shear behavior of RCA–geogrid systems under varying particle sizes (G1, G2, G3, G4), normal stresses (50, 100, 150 kPa), and shear rates (0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0 mm/min). Prediction models for interfacial shear strength and deformation are proposed. Results indicate that the interface exhibits shear softening across different particle size distributions and normal stresses. RCA with well-graded particle size distributions (G1, G2, G3) showed higher peak shear strength and friction angle, along with smaller vertical displacements, compared to poorly graded RCA (G4). While shear rate had little influence on peak shear strength, it significantly affected vertical displacement. Furthermore, predictive formulas for interface shear strength and deformation were developed considering the curvature coefficient. Since shear strength is critical in determining RCA’s capacity to resist shear forces, these findings highlight its importance for ensuring structural integrity and enhancing its application in sustainable construction.

abstract: Soil-rock mixture (SRM) is a complex geological material widely distributed in nature, and its mechanical properties are typically controlled by the block skeleton. title: Determining Young's Modulus Using a Gear-Driven Apparatus and Instrument-Correcting Methodology
abstract: Young's modulus, defined as the ratio of stress to the corresponding strain, is a key physical quantity for evaluating the elasticity of materials. Various methods have been developed to measure Young's modulus. For example, the dynamic resonance method offers high accuracy but is conceptually more complex for students to grasp compared to the more intuitive static stretching method[1]-[5]. The use of a rotational motion sensor for measuring Young's modulus is relatively straightforward, yet it is limited in application, as it is suitable primarily for measuring the Young's modulus of thin metal wires[6]. The dial gauge method is simple to operate but can be affected by contact friction, which may distort the readings[7]. In undergraduate education, the optical lever method is commonly used to measure Young's modulus due to its sensitivity and intuitive principles, providing students with a deeper understanding of Hooke's law and its practical applications[8]. Despite its advantages, this method presents challenges commonly encountered by students, particularly its susceptibility to vibration-induced measurement errors. To address these limitations, this paper describes an experimental approach using gears and a digital force sensor. This new approach offers stable measurements and a wide range of applicability, making it suitable for both instructor-led demonstrations and hands-on student experiments.

title: StitchOver: Technical Embroidery on Seamed Fabrics
journal: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)
abstract: Smart textiles embed interactivity into everyday garments, supporting use cases like always-available sensing for medical applications or sports. Machine embroidery allows integrating functionalities into existing textiles. However, embroidering onto real-world textile goods remains challenging. Textile goods are rarely made of a single homogeneous substrate of fabric, and embroidery with functional materials such as conductive threads requires machines to be more tightly calibrated than for decorative embroidery. In particular, seams, which bring together different substrates, along with machine variability, cause shifts in tension and friction between the functional thread and the textile substrate that frequently lead to defects (70% of samples in our evaluation). We present a technique to reliably embroider on seamed fabric even when using functional threads. Our software tool automatically digitizes user-defined stitch patterns by introducing what we call “ JumpStitches ” to bypass seam interference. We evaluated our approach under varying machine states (under-tensioned, well-calibrated, and over-tensioned), and across multiple seam and pattern configurations. Our results show that the JumpStitch mechanism eliminates defects, while maintaining conductivity compared to 70% defects without JumpStitches , and even in poorly calibrated machine states continues to work well.

title: Finite Element Method for Sustainable Structural Integrity of Multi-bolted Flanges: A Review of Optimized Design and Green Maintenance Strategies

title: Numerical Analysis of the Ngouache IV Landslide (Bafoussam, Cameroon) Using ABAQUS: Influence of Geotechnical Parameters
abstract: Over the past 25 years, landslides have caused substantial loss of life and damage to infrastructure in Cameroon. Among the most devastating events are the Ngouache IV landslide, which claimed more than 40 lives in October 2019, and the Mawoh landslide in Limbe, which resulted in 21 fatalities in 2001. More recently, the Dschang Cliff landslide caused multiple fatalities and severely disrupted national road traffic, underscoring the growing landslide hazard in the country. This study focuses on the Ngouache IV landslide and aims to model its failure mechanism to improve the understanding and mitigation of landslide hazards in similar geological and geomorphological settings across the country. Slope stability was evaluated through a numerical analysis that assessed the influence of key geotechnical parameters on slope behavior. The analysis was conducted using the finite element software ABAQUS. The investigated parameters include Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio, cohesion, angle of internal friction, pore-water pressure, and void ratio. Results from this parametric study indicate that besides the pore-water pressure, the Young’s modulus exerts the greatest influence on slope deformation, leading to the largest predicted ground displacement and volume of mobilized material. title: Energy-based assessment of the survivability of structural systems under accidental actions
abstract: Purpose. To develop an energy-based criterion for assessing the survivability of structural systems under accidental actions, taking into account the dynamic behavior of the structure and the mechanisms of energy dissipation. Methodology. The study was carried out using a discrete nonlinear model in which the structure is represented as a system of lumped masses and nonlinear connections. Geometric and material nonlinearities, the dynamic nature of loading, and contact interaction between elements were taken into account. The numerical implementation was performed using custom-developed Python scripts, with determination of the components of the system energy balance. The proposed approach was tested using a laboratory experiment on the dynamic behavior of a steel frame with diagonal bracing. Findings. The regularities of energy redistribution in a structural system under local damage were established, and the conditions for transition to progressive collapse were determined. journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency and irregular mechanical energy into electrical energy for self-powered sensors, wearable electronics, Internet-of-Things devices and distributed energy systems. Although major advances have been made in triboelectric materials, surface engineering and device architectures, the mechanical excitation applied during TENG testing remains an important source of experimental variability. Manual tapping, pressing and sliding can introduce uncontrolled changes in force, displacement, velocity, frequency, contact area and waveform, making comparison between experiments difficult.
