abstract: Introduction: A process is developed to deposit a coating of copper on aluminum in the form of crystalline copper nanowires growing out of the pores of anodized aluminum to completely cover the oxide surface in a self-limiting process. title: Current-driven Magnetic Skyrmions for Encoding/Storing Information: Manipulation and Dynamics in Nanoscale Structures
abstract: This dissertation investigates the dynamics of current-driven magnetic skyrmions, topological solitons in magnetic materials with broken spatial inversion symmetry, for low-power spintronic applications like racetrack memory and multilevel data storage. Skyrmions’ small size and low driving current requirements make them promising information carriers. The research examines skyrmion motion under driving currents, pinning effects, and thermal fluctuations, using numerical simulations (Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation), analytical studies (Thiele equation), and theoretical modeling to design novel data storage devices. The study analyzes skyrmion motion amidst pinning potentials from material imperfections. Simulations reveal that thermal fluctuations vary with damping: acting as a frictional force at low damping or a driving force aiding depinning at high damping. The Thiele equation quantifies this, though its accuracy wanes at low temperatures with pinning. The skyrmion Hall angle, influenced by current and pinning, provides insights for ambient-condition devices. These findings underpin a proposed multilevel data storage device, where controlled current positions skyrmions at pinning sites for high-density, low-power encoding. The research also explores altermagnetic (ATM) skyrmions, which exhibit d-wave symmetry via exchange-driven spin splitting. abstract: This study examines the mechanical behavior of a C-shaped reentrant auxetic cylindrical structure using finite element analysis (FEA) for five unit-cell configurations, with the length and height varied together (l = h) from 8 to 11 mm. title: Improving the Wear Resistance of 40Cr Steel by Multi-Pass Laser Hardening: Effect of the Number of Passes on the Microstructure, Microhardness and Tribological Properties
abstract: Laser hardening is normally applied in the solid-state regime, and the behaviour of chromium steels treated at a line energy high enough to melt the surface is far less documented. Here 40Cr steel (AISI 5140) was laser hardened at 3000 W and 5 mm/s (600 J/mm) with one, two and three passes and compared with the untreated state by roughness measurement, microhardness profiling, quantitative porosity analysis, X-ray diffraction, dry ball-on-disc sliding against a 100Cr6 ball (6 N, 3 cm/s, 200 m, n = 3) and abrasive testing to GOST 23.208-79. One pass produced a hard (530–590 HV) but porous remelted layer, with 6–9% porosity in the top 300 µm and a dislocation density of 1.6 × 1015 m−2. Repeated remelting reduced the porosity to below 1%, while the near-surface hardness fell to 280–310 HV, the dislocation density decreased four- to five-fold, and the hardened region extended to about 1300 µm, indicating tempering of the previously hardened material. After grinding and polishing, the specific wear rate of the steel in sliding fell significantly (p < 0.001) from 6.5 × 10−5 to 2.9, 4.3 and 1.7 × 10−5 mm3/(N·m), i.e., by 54, 34 and 74%, whereas the friction coefficient, 0.62–0.66, did not differ between the states. Under loose abrasive, the mass loss fell by 8.4, 25.5 and 14.3%. Three passes are recommended for sliding contacts and two passes for abrasive conditions; a single pass is not recommended because of the porosity of its remelted layer.

abstract: ABSTRACT Next‐generation biomedical implants require materials with excellent wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and biocompatibility. abstract: Gas lift transportation of deep-sea rare earth mud involves the replacement of initial water by a non-Newtonian suspension and substantial axial variation in gas content along a long riser. abstract: The increasing demand for sustainable polymer composites has led to the use of agricultural waste and natural materials as alternative reinforcements. abstract: Drilling fluids play a critical role in efficient cuttings transport, suspension of drilled solids, hydraulic performance, and wellbore stability, making rheological control essential for safe and efficient drilling operations. title: Ultrasonic-Assisted Stir Casting of SiO2-Reinforced AA7075: Microstructure, Strengthening, and Wear
abstract: Abstract The present work examines the effect of SiO2 nanoparticle addition on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and dry-sliding wear behavior of AA7075-based metal matrix nanocomposites. Four reinforcement levels, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 wt %, were investigated. AA7075 was reinforced with SiO2 using an ultrasonic-assisted stir-casting process. The process produced relatively uniform SiO2 distributions up to 1.5 wt % and a refined aluminum matrix, whereas localized particle-rich regions became evident at 2.0 wt %. The tensile strength increased from 190 ± 15 MPa for the unreinforced alloy to 255 ± 22, 310 ± 10, 360 ± 22, and 385 ± 12 MPa for composites containing 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 wt % SiO2, respectively, corresponding to strength improvements of approximately 34.2%, 63.2%, 89.5%, and 102.6%. Microhardness also increased from 86 ± 3 VHV for AA7075 to 164 ± 12 VHV for the composite containing 2.0 wt % SiO2. The improvements in strength and hardness are consistent with matrix refinement, interfacial load transfer, restriction of dislocation motion, and thermal-expansion-mismatch-induced dislocation strengthening. abstract: Rubber tracks are widely used on agricultural tractors, harvesters and lightweight field platforms due to their low ground-contact pressure, adaptability to uneven terrain and effective vibration attenuation. Under complex agricultural operating conditions with alternating soft/wet soil, straw cover, hard field ridges and gravel, tracks are subjected to combined tensioning, drive engagement, road-wheel compression, steering shear and cyclic bending, in which abrasive wear, fatigue cracking and rubber–reinforcement debonding usually develop together, critically affecting service life and reliability. Following the evidence chain of “operating condition–load–damage–life”, this review systematically summarizes the research progress on the failure mechanisms and durability of rubber tracks under complex agricultural operating conditions. It first summarizes typical service conditions and the spatial–temporal non-uniformity of track loads and the main failure modes and clarifies the many-to-many relationships between operating conditions and failures. It then analyzes damage evolution from four aspects: frictional wear and surface damage, fatigue crack initiation and propagation, rubber–reinforcement interface and composite failure, and coupling of multiple failure modes, highlighting geometric thinning, temperature rise and stiffness degradation as key feedback pathways accelerating late-stage damage. title: In the House of My Father: Kinship in the Work of Donald Rodney
abstract: Kinship is a fraught topic in the work of British artist Donald Rodney. From his earliest sketchbooks to his final exhibition, Rodney used concepts of relatedness, genealogy, and inheritance to connect his own family history with broader narratives of slavery and empire, Pan-African solidarity, and Black British identity. Prefiguring the recent interest in kinship in contemporary art and curatorial practice, Rodney explored human beings’ most intimate and enduring relationships and their enmeshment in broader patterns of affinity, mutual responsibility, and community. Yet he also highlighted pernicious uses of kinship terminology in British colonial education, nationalist politics, and citizenship law – leading to a more nuanced engagement with ideas of kinship than is prevalent in contemporary art discourse. title: DEVELOPING A METHOD FOR DETERMINING THE DECELERATION OF ELECTRIC AND HYBRID VEHICLES DURING BRAKING
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A method for determining the deceleration of electric and hybrid vehicles during braking is proposed; its relevance is supported by post-2023 statistics (over 20 million electric cars sold worldwide in 2025; 122.7 thousand registered electric vehicles in Uzbekistan by 1 July 2026). Because braking force is shared between regenerative and friction brakes in a way that depends on battery state of charge, speed and control software, the method fuses inertial, GNSS, wheel-speed and CAN-bus data with a Kalman filter and splits the total deceleration into its regenerative and friction parts. Performance is demonstrated in a simulation study; full-scale road tests remain future work.

title: Traction and Braking Performance Comparison between Manufactured and Natural Snow Track Surfaces in a Controlled Environment
abstract: ABSTRACT Prepared hard-packed tracks made from manufactured and natural snow were compared under controlled indoor conditions at approximately −8 °C and 85% relative humidity. Three tire sets were evaluated using repeated acceleration and braking tests executed by experienced test drivers. Despite similar mean compacted track index (CTI) hardness values of 83.8 and 84.9, the tracks produced clear differences in frictional performance. Mean acceleration time was 4.43 s on manufactured snow and 4.92 s on natural snow, whereas mean braking distances were 12.35 and 13.93 m, respectively, equating to 11% longer acceleration time and 13% longer braking distance on natural snow. Manufactured snow also exhibited lower within-test variability: average standard deviations on the two surfaces were 0.08 vs 0.11 s for acceleration and 0.17 vs 0.36 m for braking. Degradation measurements indicated less negative performance change on manufactured snow, although this difference was less distinct. The snow surfaces generally displayed ∼0–1% in performance change. The two tested Nordic friction tires performed similarly and outperformed the tested European friction tires on both tracks, indicating that the Nordic friction tires were more suitable for pure snow tracks. The results show that similar CTI hardness does not necessarily imply similar tire–snow performance. title: The AI Organizational Magnifier Theory: How AI Amplifies Structures, Standards, and Consequences in Organizational Talent Decisions
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: While AI adoption in organizational talent decisions has accelerated dramatically, systematic failures have emerged that existing algorithmic bias frameworks cannot fully explain: candidates silently excluded without traceability, well-intentioned diversity policies executed to their literal extreme, critical review steps optimized away by efficiency logic, and exceptional candidates systematically filtered out by historically derived success templates. This paper proposes the AI Organizational Magnifier Theory, which argues that AI systems do not independently generate organizational defects but amplify pre-existing structural capability gaps, unbounded standards, and decision consequences. The theory's meta-concept frames AI as a Brake Remover: an agent that dismantles three natural organizational braking mechanisms—the self-limiting nature of weak execution capability, the physical speed ceiling of human processing, and the temporal buffer of organizational friction. Drawing on practitioner research across 20 years and 16 Asia-Pacific markets, and four in-depth case studies, the theory identifies three pillars of amplification (structural, standards, consequence) and nine original sub-concepts. The paper proposes the governance axiom Automate elimination; retain human judgment for selection and the Verify the Tail mechanism, operationalized through a Three Gates governance framework. title: Embodied timing turns a robotic tug-of-war into cooperative transport
abstract: Living systems move loads with agents that pull against one another. Kinesin and dynein pull one vesicle, ants haul a dead insect, and antagonist muscles move a joint. Whether the timing of the forces can by itself determine which side moves the load is not well understood. Here, combining experiments, theory, and simulations of a tug-of-war between two matched teams of spring-coupled robots, we show that the relative timing of the pull forces breaks the symmetry and decides the contest. Teams pulling in unison or in strict alternation tie. Between these, the lagging team wins, most strongly near a quarter cycle, because the springs unload while the leading team coasts and the lagging team still pulls. In the model and in robot simulations, braking rather than coasting between pulls, once strong enough, shifts the advantage to the leading team. Winning and losing leave distinct signatures in each robot’s motor current. Using these local signals, we formulate an embodied decentralized phase-adaptation rule that enables transient leadership to switch between teams, allowing the collective to transport high-friction cargo and to navigate around obstacles towards a prescribed target without explicit communication.

title: Hardware-In-The-Loop Pid-Based Speed Regulation of A Dc Motor Under Variable Mechanical Load
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This study presents a Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) closed-loop speed regulation of a physical DCmotor using a LabVIEW-based PID controller. In DC motors, maintaining the desired speed under changingmechanical loading is an important control problem in electromechanical systems, where variations in loadtorque result in speed deviations and transient disturbances. An optical quadrature encoder provides real-time shaft speed feedback, and a variable friction brake isemployed to introduce controlled mechanical load disturbances. A discrete-time mathematical motor model isincorporated as a supporting simulation tool for controller development and analysis, while the physical DCmotor remains the experimental plant. title: Dedicated Hybrid Engines: Pathways from Otto Cycle to beyond 50% BTE
abstract: Dedicated Hybrid Engines (DHEs) represent a paradigm shift: engine’s purpose designed to operate within electrified powertrains, enabling them to achieve brake thermal efficiencies (BTE) of 45% and beyond – a level once considered unattainable for spark ignition (SI) engines. This chapter traces the technological evolution from the classic Otto cycle to today’s highly optimized DHEs. It explains how the Atkinson/Miller cycle, combined with advanced combustion strategies such as lean burn, cooled exhaust gas recirculation, and prechamber ignition, synergize with hybrid electrification to dramatically improve efficiency. Key enabling technologies – including high compression ratio, friction reduction, thermal management, and novel ignition systems – are examined through industrial case studies. It discusses the compatibility of DHEs with carbon neutral fuels (ethanol, synthetic fuels, hydrogen, etc.), positioning them as a cornerstone of sustainable mobility well into the future. Furthermore, data oriented approach for controls is explored to tackle uncertain dynamics through physics informed neural network (PINN) to further raise the engine performance. title: Hydrogen-bond-mediated island-chain interfacial structure for enhanced tribological performance of sugarcane bagasse/epoxy composites
abstract: The inherent brittleness and poor wear resistance of epoxy resin (EP) limit its industrial applications. Herein, sugarcane bagasse (BG) was used as a reinforcing filler in BG/EP composites. The effects of BG particle size and content on the mechanical and tribological properties of the composites were systematically investigated. The composite containing 19 wt% of 300–400 mesh BG exhibited a tensile strength of 83.1 MPa and a toughness of 19.6 MJ m −3 , representing increases of 27.6% and approximately 9.7%, respectively, compared with pure EP. Its wear rate was reduced by 96.4%. Scanning electron microscopy showed that BG was uniformly dispersed and embedded in the EP matrix, with close interfacial contact. Energy decomposition and hydrogen-bond statistics from molecular dynamics simulations indicated that hydrogen bonding and van der Waals interactions enhanced the interfacial bonding between the fibers and the matrix. This “island-chain” reinforcement mechanism (dispersed BG domains connected by hydrogen-bond-mediated interfacial interactions) facilitates stress distribution and suppresses microcrack propagation during wear. Preliminary laboratory-scale application tests showed that, following 60 min of cumulative polishing, the mass loss of the 19 wt% BG/EP polishing disc was 53.7% and 45.6% lower than that of the pure EP disc and the commercial resin-based polishing disc, respectively. title: Performance and emission analysis of sustainable rice bran-Calophyllum-CNSL biodiesel blends in a conventional diesel engine
abstract: Diesel engines are often run on blended fuels to evaluate the adaptability and alternative energy source with changing engine components. The study compares the engine performance and emission characteristics of diesel engines operating on pure diesel and biodiesel blends. Tests were carried out on a single cylinder, four stroke, water cooled direct injection diesel engine at constant speed of 1500 rpm. The 10%, 20% and 30% bio-oils by volume (B10, B20 and B30) biodiesel blends were tested at different engine loads in comparison to regular diesel without any engine modifications. The diesel engine performance was evaluated by brake power (BP), brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC), total fuel consumption (TFC) and brake thermal efficiency (BTE). Also, emissions characteristics such as carbon dioxide (CO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx) and unburned hydrocarbons (UBHC) were measured. The results revealed that all the biodiesel blends had the same braking power for all the fuels with a maximum value of 4.26KW under all loads. Because biodiesel has a reduced calorific value, performances like TFC and BSFC improved with its presence; this impact was particularly noticeable for the B30 mix. Nevertheless, the B20 blend achieved a slight increase in TFC at medium and higher loads, leading to effective fuel use. title: Performance, Emission Characteristics, and Multi-Response Optimization of BaTiO3-Enhanced Cottonseed Biodiesel in a Diesel Engine
abstract: In this study, the effects of adding barium titanate (BaTiO3) nanoparticles to a cottonseed biodiesel and diesel blend on engine performance and exhaust emissions were experimentally investigated and evaluated using multiple response optimization. Fifty, 100, and 150 mg/L BaTiO3 were added to the D70CS30 (30% cottonseed biodiesel + 70% diesel) blend, which consisted of 70% diesel and 30% biodiesel by volume. Experiments were conducted on a single-cylinder, direct-injection diesel engine at a constant speed of 3000 rpm and six load levels ranging from 0.5 to 3.0 kW. Brake specific fuel consumption, brake thermal efficiency, CO, HC, CO2, and NOx results were modeled using the response surface method. While engine load showed a dominant effect on all responses, the nanoparticle effects exhibited concentration-dependent nonlinear variations. title: Influence of eco-friendly diesel fuel additives on fuel properties, engine performance and exhaust emissions
abstract: Diesel fuel used in transport, marine applications, and stationary power systems is vulnerable to storage-related degradation, especially in the presence of bio-components, which creates a need for environmentally benign additives that preserve fuel quality without compromising engine operation. This study investigates the effect of four eco-friendly diesel additives—liquid Effective Microorganisms EM(F), ceramic EM carriers EM(C), silver solution (SS), and colloidal nanosilver (CNS)—on fuel properties, engine performance, and exhaust emissions. Fuel blends were prepared at additive concentrations of 1, 2, and 5% v/v for physicochemical analyses, while engine tests were performed for selected blends at 2 and 5% using an SW 680/1 direct-injection diesel engine operating at 20 and 30 kW. The novelty of the study lies in the integrated assessment of environmentally oriented additives as potential alternatives to conventional fuel-treatment agents through combined evaluation of ignition quality, density, distillation characteristics, low-temperature behavior, corrosion tendency, fuel consumption, thermal efficiency, and exhaust emissions. title: A Modular System for Sampling and Measuring Non-Exhaust Particles of Light-Duty Vehicles in On-Road Testing
abstract: Abstract Non-exhaust particles contribute increasingly to road transport emissions, but consistent on-road measurement methods for brake and tyre particles are missing. This work introduces a modular system designed to sample and measure non-exhaust particles from light-duty vehicles in on-road testing. The goal was to create a flexible configuration requiring minimal adaptation, starting from a semi-enclosed system for brake particle sampling and validated through lab and road tests. It was then upgraded to a fully enclosed setup for brake particles and adapted for tyre particle collection by modifying the sampling nozzle. The full enclosure isolates the brake system from environmental interference, while the nozzle change enables tyre particle sampling. The modular system supports comprehensive testing of non-exhaust emissions and contributes to the development of reliable emission factors.

title: Train Energy Simulations
abstract: Rail decarbonisation requires a shift from diesel to low- or zero-carbon energy. Locomotive and tender design involves many factors like energy-storage mass and volume, driveline efficiency, adhesion, braking capability, and route-specific demand. Longitudinal train dynamics (LTD)–based energy simulation provides a system-level method for evaluating these interactions. This chapter estimates train energy usage and compares zero-emission traction options, linking traction technology and train operation to the performance requirements of specific routes.

title: Effects of Pyrolysis Fuel Blend, Ethanol-Pentanol Additives, and Injection Pressure Variations on Diesel Engine Performance
journal: R E M (Rekayasa Energi Manufaktur) Jurnal
abstract: Diesel engines have high thermal efficiency and produce substantial torque, making them widely used across various sectors. However, dependence on fossil fuels and increasing exhaust emissions have driven the need for the development of more environmentally friendly alternative fuels. One of the solutions being developed is the utilization of pyrolysis oil derived from plastic waste as an alternative fuel. Nevertheless, the use of pyrolysis oil still has limitations in combustion quality, thereby requiring the addition of additives. This study was conducted experimentally using a single-cylinder diesel engine operated at a constant speed of 1500 rpm under load variations of 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 and 3000 W. The tested fuels included solar diesel fuel, a P20 blend (20% plastic waste pyrolysis oil and 80% diesel fuel), and P20 blends supplemented with ethanol and pentanol at specified proportions. The performance parameters evaluated were brake power, torque, Brake Thermal Efficiency (BTE), Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC), and smoke oppacity. The research findings showed that increasing the injection pressure from 180 to 210 bar improved engine performance and reduced emissions across all fuel blends. title: Hybrid Train: Validation Process and Experimentation Insights Regarding Decarbonization and Operation Robustness
abstract: Abstract Régiolis Hybrid project involves modifying an existing dual-mode Régiolis train by replacing 2 of the 4 powerpacks with high-power lithium-ion batteries. The main aim of this project is to reduce energy consumption by 20% by recovering and exploiting electrical braking energy, previously dissipated as heat in the braking choppers. For the first time in France, a train equipped with Li-Ion batteries was able to carry passengers. Fitted with a datalogger that continuously sends all the necessary monitoring data, it then travelled more than 60,000 km, enabling a precise assessment of the overall performance. Environmental performance was measured by a test bench campaign to replay the data collected during commercial operation. This made it possible to assess the precise gain in CO2 emissions and pollutants without bias, and find up to −25% CO2, −52% HC, −41% CO, −41% NOx, −39% PM. Furthermore, performance with biofuels was also evaluated. Finally, reliability was studied from two angles: the ability to keep the timetable compared to the rest of the dual-mode trains fleet, but also by analyzing the new operating points of the remaining powerpacks to ensure that the usage profile doesn’t degrade the train reliability.

title: Cymbopogon citrates a Biodegradable waste-derived biodiesel as a potential green fuel: Process Extraction and Utilization in Agricultural Diesel Engine
abstract: This study investigates the use of two specific alcohols, octanol and deconal, alongside diesel and biodiesel derived from Cymbopogon citratus. Two ternary blends, labeled as D50-CC30-OCT20 and D50-CC30-DEC20, were formulated and analyzed to assess their engine performance compared to the D50-CC50 blend, pure diesel operation. Results indicate a decrease in peak cylinder pressure with the use of ternary blends. The maximum rate of heat release was observed to be higher in the octanol-containing blend. Furthermore, the deconal blend exhibited a 2.5% improvement in brake thermal efficiency (BTE) compared to octanol yet remained 3.5% lower than traditional diesel operation. Notably, the NOx emissions of the deconal blend were 4% lower compared to octanol. Overall, higher alcohol blends led to reduced smoke emissions compared to binary blends. Octanol, specifically, showed a 15% decrease in smoke opacity. However, the emissions of hydrocarbons (HC) and carbon monoxide (CO) increased with the use of greater alcohol blends. This research underscores the potential of 1-deconal as a viable fuel option for diesel engines running on biodiesel derived from Cymbopogon citratus oil sourced from biomass.

title: Evaluating Flexibility and Assets in Battery-Powered Train Operations: A Simulation Approach
abstract: Abstract The transition to decarbonized railway rolling stock fleets, such as battery-powered regional trains, presents significant challenges for rail operations, yet offers substantial benefits, including reductions in CO 2 emissions and energy gains through direct brake energy recovery. Their operational benefits are often undervalued. This research aims to perform a comprehensive analysis of the flexibility provided by battery trains amidst operational uncertainties, such as discontinuity or total absence of electrification in contrast to conventional Electrical Multiple Units (EMU) trains. A state-of-the-art review of these operational uncertainties has been conducted to define test scenarios. The analysis is grounded in simulations using a validated energy model and applies a numerical simulation prediction model for range estimation, which integrates the conditions of rolling stock, infrastructure, and operational elements within the railway system. The analysis conducted herein validates a single Battery Electrical Multiple Units (BEMU) significant operational flexibility across the simulated cases, especially its ability to ensure operational continuity during power supply failures and simultaneously recover from delays, a key advantage over conventional EMUs. These findings warrant the initiation of furthermore structured and operationally oriented research aimed at bridging the gap between simulation and real-world deployment.

title: Characterizing hydrogen-diesel dual-fuel combustion in a commercial heavy-duty vehicle
abstract: Hydrogen-diesel dual-fuel (H₂DF) combustion is a promising pathway for reducing CO₂ emissions from conventional diesel engines, particularly in heavy-duty applications. However, most existing studies are based on engine dynamometer experiments under idealized steady-state conditions, leaving gaps in understanding the constraints of real-world operation and implementation. This study addresses these gaps through an experimental investigation of a retrofit H₂DF system implemented on a commercial heavy-duty vehicle. The objective is to identify the governing factors and mechanisms of H₂DF combustion and their relationships with engine operating parameters under representative conditions. A research vehicle equipped with a retrofit H₂DF system, where hydrogen is injected upstream of the intake manifold, was tested on a chassis dynamometer under steady-state conditions to compare H₂DF and conventional diesel operation and to identify H₂DF combustion regimes. The vehicle was then evaluated under real-world traffic conditions to assess in-use performance and compare results with steady-state testing. Five distinct H₂DF combustion regimes were identified and mapped, providing a generalized framework for characterizing H₂DF combustion under varying operating conditions. The governing factors and transition thresholds between regimes were determined, defining the operational space and associated trade-offs among emissions and efficiency. title: Techno-Economic and Lifecycle Comparative Analysis of Strong Hybrid Electric Vehicles (SHEVs) and Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs) in Emerging Automotive Markets
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The transition toward sustainable passenger mobility in emerging markets has created a sharp technological and economic divide between Strong Hybrid Electric Vehicles (SHEVs)—specifically Series-Parallel power-split architectures—and Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs). While BEVs eliminate tailpipe emissions and offer low per-kilometer energy costs, widespread adoption remains constrained by high upfront battery capital costs, steep commercial fast-charging tariffs, secondary-market depreciation, and coal-heavy electricity grids. Conversely, SHEVs pair Atkinson-cycle internal combustion engines with self-charging electric drivetrains to achieve brake thermal efficiencies exceeding 40%and real-world fuel economies of 23" to " 28" km/l" without relying on external charging infrastructure. title: Behavioural-Aware Geofencing and the Possibilities of Its Implementation in Micromobility; A Conceptual Model
abstract: Abstract The rapid rise of micro-mobility options, including e-scooters and bike-sharing, has reshaped urban transport patterns. Micro-mobility options can potentially reduce emissions, improve accessibility, and provide a better experience in the first - and last-mile connectivity within cities, especially in collaboration with other transportation means like Public Transport in multimodal Hubs. However, its rapid adoption has led to significant operational and regulatory concerns, including safety (unsafe riding behavior), improper parking, dynamic demand, damage to vehicles, and inefficiencies in operations. These challenges affect both public safety and the long-term viability of micro-mobility services. This paper , developed in the context of the BIO-INTEL-MOB project proposes a conceptual behavior-aware dynamic geofencing framework to address persistent safety and compliance problems in shared micromobility—sidewalk riding, wrong-way travel, red-light violations, instability events, and low helmet use—that static, geography-only rules poorly manage. title: High-resolution Modeling of Coronae and Winds in Solar-type Stars with Varying Rotation Rates. II. Stellar Winds
abstract: Abstract Observations suggest a connection between steady-wind mass loss and coronal X-ray activity in low-mass main-sequence stars. Interpreting this connection is challenging because the wind is controlled mainly by the large-scale open field, whereas X-ray emission traces heating in small-scale closed fields often unresolved in global wind models. Here we use Space Weather Modeling Framework–Alfvén-Wave Solar Model with global convective dynamo-generated magnetic maps and solar magnetograms. We model Alfvén-wave-heated winds for four solar-type stars plus the Sun, spanning rotation rates of 1.0–23.3 times the solar rate, and magnetic field strengths of 6.0–1200 G. Our models show that faster rotation yields a more tightly wound spiral, a larger Alfvén surface, higher terminal wind speeds, and a harsher wind-pressure environment for orbiting exoplanets, different from that of the present-day Sun. We estimate the mass- and angular-momentum-loss rates and find systematic differences from Zeeman–Doppler imaging based predictions. Building on the successful reproduction of X-ray coronae in our Paper I, we obtain the first self-consistent activity–wind relation in a unified modeling framework: the mass-loss rate scales with the surface X-ray flux following a power law with an index of ∼0.67. It asks whether a fleet of physically modular, unoccupied scaled vehicles can cooperate in controlled module transfer and transport scheduling without concealing loss of material identity, mechanical safety or human stop authority. Its central three-coupling is Vehicle Cooperation x Module Reconfiguration x Mobility Systems. Physical experiments are proposed only for enclosed small-scale test beds, certified material coupons, hardware-in-the-loop fleet schedules and independently metered docking stations. No integrated public-road vehicle, passenger application, vehicle type approval or automatic nano-to-car scale transfer is asserted. The falsifiable candidate compares a frozen distributed cooperative exchange architecture against competent fixed-body fleet dispatch, centralized modular scheduling and metered teleoperated docking with the same material, energy, operator, station, sensing, communication and computation resources. A proposed service advantage must survive the entire population of requested jobs and attempted exchanges. The source's selective-risk model, R_sel(tau) = E[L(yhat,y) given c >= tau], is retained but always reported together with accepted-task coverage; refusing difficult requests cannot count as safety or efficiency progress.
